summary.text: 北 means “north.” Its ancient form is interpreted as two people turned back-to-back. The graph was used for “north” by Shang-period writing; the proposed explanation is that it was borrowed for a different, similar-sounding word. The older word and exact sound match are not established.

formation.text: The whole graph is pictographic: it depicts two human figures turned away from each other. This picture does not itself mean “north.” The proposed earlier sense “turn against” or “turn one’s back” is inferred from the image and later uses, rather than securely attested in excavated writing.

components.text: 北 is treated as one indivisible picture of two people facing away from each other. Its paired forms are not analyzed here as separate modern components, and no sound element within the graph is established.

history.text: Oracle-bone and later script examples are reported. The back-to-back conception is described as continuing through the seal-script form, with changes in stroke execution; the selected oracle-style and seal-style images illustrate these forms but are modern redrawings, not artifact photographs.

A Han dictionary glosses 北 with a term understood as “turning away” or “contrary” and analyzes the graph as two people back-to-back. This is a Han-period account, not independent proof of the graph’s earliest use.

Around the Qin–Han transition, 北 was still used to write “back” as 背 began to distinguish that word in writing. 背 combines 肉, the flesh element, with 北 as a sound element; by the Eastern Han, 背 had become the usual graph for “back.” This describes a change in writing, not when the spoken word began.

uncertainties.text: The proposed original sense “turn against” or “turn one’s back” is inferred from the graphic conception and later uses; the study identifies no secure excavated example writing that sense. The exact chronology of the proposed senses and their semantic links remains unresolved.

The reported Shang-period use for “north” is explained as reuse of the graph for a different word because of a proposed sound similarity. The old word or object-name and its pronunciation are not recoverable here, so this borrowing account remains a proposal; it does not show that “north” developed in meaning from “back.”

senses.period: Shang period onward (reported); exact first occurrence unresolved
senses.text: 北 is reported as a loan graph for the direction “north” from Shang-period writing, and this became its principal continuing function. A specific earliest inscription context is not supplied.

senses.gloss: turn against; turn one’s back on
senses.text: This proposed sense is associated with the back-to-back image and the Han dictionary gloss, but secure excavated examples writing it have not been identified.

senses.period: Qin–Han written use reported; spoken-sense chronology unresolved
senses.text: 北 was used to write “back”; 背 later became the usual graph. This change in written practice does not establish when the spoken word arose or prove a semantic path from “turn against.”

senses.period: Qin–Han written examples reported; exact chronology unresolved
senses.text: Written examples of 北 for “back side” are reported. Their attestation does not establish when the spoken sense developed or its precise relation to other proposed senses.

developments.text: A semantic connection is proposed, but the earlier sense is not securely attested and the written examples do not establish the chronology of spoken meanings.

The reported Shang-period use for “north” is explained as reuse of the graph for a different word because of a proposed sound similarity. The old word’s name and sound comparison are unavailable; this is a proposed borrowing, not a demonstrated meaning change from “back” to “north.”

limitations.text: Shang-period use for “north” is reported, but no specific earliest inscription context is supplied. The hypothesized original sense, the exact order of the proposed meanings, and the links among them remain unresolved.

overview.text: 北 means “north.” Its ancient form is interpreted as two people turned back-to-back. The graph was reused for “north” because of a proposed sound similarity, though the old word and exact match are unknown.

components.text: Read 北 as one paired picture of two people turned away from each other. The proposed older “turn against” sense is an interpretation, not a securely attested earliest meaning.

takeaway.text: “North” is explained as a sound-based borrowing, not as a meaning clearly developed from “back.”
